## Introductions

- PhD Statistics University of St Andrews (Scotland)
- NIMBLE Development Team [here](https://r-nimble.org/)
- Work on computational statistics (e.g. approximate posterior distributions, MCMC methods, efficient matrix exponentiation)
- R packages `nimbleQuad` and `spbal`

## Why RTMB

- R wrapper for TMB
- Convert R code to C++ for speed
- Automatic Differentiation
- Integrate out random effects (e.g. Laplace)
- Code can run in basic R for checking

## Course Structure

- Can't code if you don't understand model
- Focus on understanding a model, then coding it in RTMB
- Will focus on understanding in the mornings and practical coding in the afternoon

## Learning Outcomes

- Understand how to fit a custom likelihood and report on it
- Basic programming in RTMB
- Fitting a random effects model
- Useful RTMB tricks

## Outline Day 1

1. (9:00 – 9:50) Welcome and course introduction, introduction to maximum likelihood estimation, and assignment review.
2. (10:00 - 10:50) Writing and fitting a stock recruit likelihood in R. Improve that likelihood with RTMB and compare. Compare with standard R packages. 
3. (11:00 – 11:50) Introduction to RTMB and automatic differentiation (AD). Compare AD with finite differencing. What is a gradient and a Hessian. 
4. (13:00 – 13:50) Add random effects to your likelihood. Laplace and RTMB 
5. (14:00 – 14:50) Practice writing likelihoods with random effects and fit them. Hierarchical stock recruitment models.  Compare output with `glmmTMB`.
6. (15:00 – 16:30) Additional random effect structures (e.g. time varying productivity). 

## Outline Day 2

1. (9:00 – 9:50) Variance estimation for maximum likelihood. Delta method to approximate parameters. Using RTMB to report variance and confidence intervals. 
2. (10:00 – 10:50) RTMB functionality. Learn little details about how to use RTMB effectively. 
3. (11:00 – 11:50) Writing helper functions and atomics (e.g. Lambert W). Best coding practices. 
4. (13:00 – 16:30) Practice writing complex likelihood functions in RTMB 

## PDF

- Random variable $x$
- Probability mass function $p(x)$ if $x$ is discrete

```{r}
x <- 0:20
px <- dbinom(x, size = 20, prob = 0.25)
plot(x, px, ylab = "p(x)", xlab = "x", col = "black", lwd = 3, type = "h")
```

- Probability density function $f(x)$ if $x$ is continuous.
- $f(x)$ describes a density, not a probability of an event.
- Probability defined by some area under the curve, e.g.
$$
  p(x \leq 1)= \int_{-\infty}^1 f(x)dx
$$

```{r}
x <- seq(-5, 5, by = 0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, 0, 1)
plot(x, fx, ylab = "f(x)", xlab = "x", type = "l")
polygon(c(x[x <= 1], 1, 0), c(fx[x <= 1], 0, 0), col="blue", border=NA)
```

## Expectation

- Expected value of $x$ (or mean) when discrete
$$
  \mathbb{E}(x) = \sum xp(x)
$$
```{r, echo = TRUE}
  mean(rbinom(10000, size = 10, prob = 0.25))
  sum((0:10)*dbinom(0:10, size = 10, prob = 0.25))
```

- Expected value of $x$ (or mean) when continuous
$$
  \mathbb{E}(x) = \int xf(x)dx
$$
```{r, echo = TRUE}
  mean(rgamma(10000, 1, 2))
  integrate(\(x){x*dgamma(x,1,2)}, lower=0, upper=Inf)$value
```

- Sample mean
$$
  \mathbb{E}(x) = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}
$$

## Variance

- Definition of variance is difference of squared expectation and expectation squared.
$$
  Var(x) = \mathbb{E}(x^2) - \mathbb{E}(x)^2.
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
  var(rgamma(10000, 1, 2))
  integrate(\(x){x^2*dgamma(x,1,2)}, lower=0, upper=Inf)$value - (1/2)^2
```

- Sample variance
$$
  Var(x) = \frac{(\sum x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}
$$

## Joint Density

- Some sample $\textbf{x}$, of size $n$
- Assume $x_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$
- If we assume all are independent, then the joint density is
$$
  f(\textbf{x}) = f(x_1, \ldots, f_n) = f(x_1)f(x_2) \cdots f(x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)
$$

## Likelihood

- For some parameters $\mathbf{\theta} = \{\mu, \sigma\}$
- Likelihood is the data joint density expressed in terms of the parameters, conditional on the data.
- $L(\mathbf{\theta} | \textbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)$
- Maximum likelihood estimation -- Find maximum values of parameters given the data.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "100%"

x <- rnorm(100, 0.25, 2)
ll <- function(mu_vector) {
  sapply(mu_vector, function(m) {
    sum(dnorm(x, mean = m, sd = 2, log = TRUE))
  })
}
mu <- seq(-5, 5, 0.1)

plot(mu, ll(mu), xlab = "mu", ylab = "ll", main = "Log-Likelihood", type = "l")

plot(mu, -ll(mu), xlab = "mu", ylab = "nll", main = "Negative Log-Likelihood", type = "l")
```

## Optimization in R

- Gradient is the slope (derivative) in terms of the parameters
- Gradient based methods optimization uses slope to find max/min
- Random start, evaluate objective function, use gradient to move to new value
- Run until at maximum/minimum (where gradient is zero)
- Examples are `optim` or `nlminb`
- If gradient not provided, then finite differences are used.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
set.seed(24)
x <- rnorm(100, 0.25, 2)
nll <- \(pars){
  mu <- pars[1]
  sigma <- exp(pars[2])
  -sum(dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
}

optim(c(0,0), nll)
# nlminb(c(0,0), nll)
```
